planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in warm, slightly moist potting mix or water; new growth typically appears within four to six weeks.

directions: A Brazilian forest-floor native in the pepper family, this compact rosette-former carries rounded, quilted, pewter-gray leaves veined in deep green and set on slender, wine-red petioles, giving a metallic sheen distinct from the more deeply ruffled caperata types. Grow in bright, indirect light away from direct sun, which can scorch the thin leaf surface despite its succulent-feeling thickness. Let the top inch or two of the mix dry between waterings, since the fleshy leaves and stems store water and rot quickly in soggy soil. Its small, tidy scale suits shelves, terrariums, and dish gardens where its silvery foliage contrasts well with plain-green companions.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf-petiole or stem cuttings rooted in moist potting mix; established plants also benefit from division of crowded clumps.

directions: Native to Brazilian rainforest understories, this species produces broad, heart-shaped, gray-green leaves patterned with darker marbled veining and carried on reddish, upright stems, making it a favorite of specialty houseplant collectors distinct from the smaller-leaved caperata and griseoargentea types. Provide bright, indirect light; too little light causes the marbled pattern to fade toward plain green, while direct sun bleaches the leaf surface. Allow the soil to dry noticeably between waterings, as the semi-succulent leaves and stems are prone to rot in constantly damp mix. Its broad, patterned foliage makes it a strong textural accent among finer-leaved shade houseplants on a bright windowsill or plant shelf.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings with a leaf node in moist potting mix or water; cuttings establish readily and quickly form trailing stems.

directions: This trailing cultivar carries narrow, lance-shaped, semi-succulent leaves striped with a broad central band of creamy white against dark green margins, giving a bold, high-contrast look distinct from the plainer trailing peperomias already common in cultivation. Grow in bright, indirect light, which keeps the white banding crisp; low light causes the variegated stripe to dull toward green. Let the top inch of the mix dry between waterings, since the fleshy leaves store moisture and are prone to rot if kept constantly wet. Its cascading stems suit small hanging pots, shelves, or the edge of a mixed shade container where the striped foliage can trail freely.
